summary:
Piura has no statute, enforcement record or incident specific to trans visitors in the audited sources; the national framework of Peru is the whole of what is documented, and it binds Piura as national legislation. Nothing in the record marks Piura as either an aggravation of, or a refuge from, that framework, and no local mitigation is documented.

The central mechanism is a national restriction on restroom access. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the draft also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the Jorge Chávez airport in Lima, so the law's own origin story indicates which everyday act it polices. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote; its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject to narrow listed exceptions. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same rule and additionally bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement is expected to rest on staff judgment at the door. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and states there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Legal gender recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation, which is what makes a document check a live risk of outing. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

The legal basis of the restriction is contested. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, holds that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP separately found the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

One case reached a judgment. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's domestic restriction runs against the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which treats gender identity as protected personal autonomy and obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights; IDEHPUCP's analysis makes the same argument from article 2(2) of the Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The conflict between the two layers is unresolved in the sources.

On hate-crime coverage Peru sits with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American countries without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, a comparison that situates the 2017 repeal regionally rather than as an isolated event.

The Azul Rojas Marín judgment is described by BBC News Mundo as the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which indicates the route a visitor-side complaint would have to travel and how long it takes: nearly 20 years and years of litigation for a case with named defendants.

Turbulence in the legislative layer is visible in the sequence of the bathroom bills: committee approval in February 2025, plenary approval with exemption from a second vote on 2 April 2025, and the wider package enacted in April 2025, alongside a July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling that struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist challenge.
localsOnly:
Residents of Piura live under the same national rules as visitors, but with continuous exposure rather than a single trip: article 5 of the April 2025 law governs everyday use of public sanitary services, and the ban on inclusive signage removes 'women in their diversity' from public and commercial premises.

For residents the enforcement risk is concentrated in routine settings where staff control access and may ask for documents, including gyms, where a consumer-protection body has already dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Residents have no hate-crime protection on the basis of LGBT identity following the 2017 repeal of those provisions from the Penal Code, carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition claiming one million signatures.

Resident-facing censorship exposure comes from the vague child-protection articles of the April 2025 law, including the article 4 ban on media and advertising content, which reaches identity, artistic and educational material; the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Healthcare access improved on one axis in June 2024, when Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Legal gender recognition itself remains long, costly and invasive for residents, which is why identity documents commonly fail to match presentation.

Residents can still litigate: an activist legal challenge produced the July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling that an anti-equality decree was unconstitutional, and IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru publishes legal analysis of the restroom provisions for use in that kind of challenge.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Piura-specific statute, enforcement record, complaint, court decision or incident involving a trans person appears in the audited sources. Whether municipal authorities, regional health services or police in Piura have issued guidance implementing article 5, or have declined to, is unresolved and not sourced.

The claim that enforcement rests on identity-document checks at restroom doors is an expectation stated by activist Gianna Camacho, not an observed enforcement pattern; no documented case of a document check, refusal of entry or arrest under article 5 in Piura or elsewhere in Peru is in the sources.

The scale of document mismatch is not quantified anywhere in the inventory: no figure is available for how many trans people in Peru hold identity documents inconsistent with their presentation, or for how many visitors would present such documents at a border or checkpoint.

The 2024 hate-crime figures are acknowledged by their own co-author to be a sub-registry, and the 54 killings recorded between 2020 and 2023 are therefore a floor rather than a count. No geographic breakdown of those killings by department is sourced, so Piura's share is unknown.

Whether the July 2025 constitutional court ruling or Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 can be used to challenge article 5 is unresolved in the sources; no challenge to the restroom provision itself is recorded.

Whether the exceptions in the February 2025 committee text survived into the version approved by the Plenary on 2 April 2025 is not stated; IDEHPUCP refers to narrow listed exceptions without enumerating them.
